title: Elementary Idea of the Quantum Mechanical Model — de Broglie's Wave Equation
topicTitle: Elementary idea of quantum mechanical model: de Broglie's wave equation
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Matter Learns to Wave

Bohr postulated quantisation; de Broglie (1924) **derived** it. If light — a wave — can behave as particles (photoelectric effect), then particles — electrons — should behave as waves. An electron wave can circle the nucleus only if a **whole number of wavelengths fits the orbit**; that condition *is* Bohr's quantisation, no longer arbitrary. This single idea, developed by Schrödinger into the wave equation, replaced orbits with **orbitals** and opened the quantum mechanical model.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 The de Broglie relation

Every moving particle has a wavelength:

**λ = h / mv = h / p** (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)

- For **macroscopic** objects m is large → λ is absurdly small → wave nature is undetectable.
- For an **electron** (m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg) at ordinary speeds λ ≈ 10⁻¹⁰ m — atomic dimensions — so wave behaviour shows.

### 2.2 Deriving Bohr's quantisation (the 3m chain)

1. An electron wave must be a **standing wave** on its orbit — otherwise it destructively interferes with itself and dies.
2. Standing-wave condition: circumference = whole number of wavelengths → **2πr = nλ**.
3. Substitute λ = h/mv: 2πr = nh/mv → **mvr = nh/2π** — exactly Bohr's quantisation of angular momentum.

### 2.3 Experimental proof — Davisson and Germer (1927)

Electrons fired at a **nickel crystal** were **diffracted**, producing a diffraction pattern like X-rays — direct proof that electrons diffract as waves, with the wavelength matching de Broglie's prediction. (Thomson's electron diffraction through thin films confirmed it independently.)

### 2.4 The quantum mechanical model (elementary idea)

- Schrödinger's wave equation treats the electron as a **standing wave in three dimensions**.
- Its solutions, **wave functions ψ**, describe **orbitals** — regions of **high probability** (ψ²) of finding the electron.
- Energy is still quantised; the definite orbit is replaced by a probability cloud obeying the uncertainty principle.
- Four quantum numbers (n, l, mₗ, mₛ) label each solution.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **de Broglie wavelength** | λ = h/mv — the wave length of any moving particle | Inversely proportional to momentum |
| **Standing wave** | A wave whose pattern is fixed because a whole number of wavelengths fits the boundary | The orbit condition 2πr = nλ |
| **Wave function (ψ)** | Solution of the Schrödinger equation for an electron | ψ itself has no physical meaning |
| **Orbital** | Region where the probability of finding the electron (ψ²) is high | Replaces Bohr's orbit |
| **Probability density (ψ²)** | Square of the wave function — likelihood per unit volume | What orbitals display |
| **Heisenberg uncertainty** | Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π | Why orbits must become orbitals |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Worked numerical — wavelength of an electron (NEB-style template)

**Q: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving with a velocity of 10⁶ m s⁻¹.**
λ = h/mv = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / (9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 10⁶) = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / 9.1 × 10⁻²⁵ = **7.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ m ≈ 0.73 nm** — comparable to atomic spacing, which is why crystals diffract electrons.

### 4.2 Worked numerical — the cricket ball contrast

**Q: Find the wavelength of a 150 g cricket ball at 40 m s⁻¹.**
λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / (0.150 × 40) = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / 6 = **1.1 × 10⁻³⁴ m** — smaller than any measurable length by 20 orders of magnitude: macroscopic wave nature is unobservable. This contrast is the favourite NEB application question.

### 4.3 Why only certain orbits survive

An orbit where the circumference is 2.5λ (say) would overlap crests on troughs — the wave cancels itself. Only orbits with 2πr = nλ reinforce; hence discrete radii, discrete energies, discrete spectrum. Quantisation is geometry, not decree.

### 4.4 From ψ to orbitals

The Schrödinger equation ψ solutions depend on three quantum numbers (n, l, mₗ); each allowed combination is one **orbital** with a characteristic shape (s spherical, p dumbbell). ψ² gives the probability picture. Bohr's radius r = 0.529 n² Å survives only as the **most probable distance** of the 1s electron — not a track.

### Deep dive — the wave nature of matter and the standing-wave derivation

de Broglie (1924) argued by symmetry: if light waves can behave as particles (photoelectric effect), particles should behave as waves, with λ = h/p = h/mv. For macroscopic objects the wavelength is absurdly small (a 100 g ball at 10 m/s: λ ≈ 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ m), but for an electron accelerated through 100 V, λ ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁰ m — atomic dimensions, which is why electron diffraction (Davisson–Germer, 1927) shows ring patterns exactly like X-rays.

The derivation NEB loves: Bohr's rule mvr = nh/2π follows if the electron wave must form a standing wave around the orbit — nλ = 2πr with λ = h/mv gives mvr = nh/2π. Quantisation is no longer a postulate but a boundary condition, the same one that fixes guitar-string frequencies. This is also why orbitals have nodes: a wave confined to an atom can only vibrate in allowed patterns.

**Wave behaviour — where you see it and where you don't**

| Particle | Speed | de Broglie λ | Wave effects visible? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Electron (100 eV) | ~5.9 × 10⁶ m/s | ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁰ m | Yes — Davisson–Germer diffraction |
| H₂ molecule at 300 K | ~1900 m/s | ≈ 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m | Yes — governs quantum states |
| Dust particle (10⁻⁹ g, 1 mm/s) | 10⁻³ m/s | ≈ 6.6 × 10⁻²² m | No — far below any slit size |
| Cricket ball (150 g, 30 m/s) | 30 m/s | ≈ 1.5 × 10⁻³⁴ m | No — utterly negligible |

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Wave vs particle behaviour**

| Basis | Wave behaviour | Particle behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| Evidence | Diffraction, interference | Photoelectric effect, collisions |
| Light shows | Yes (Young's double slit) | Yes (Einstein, photons) |
| Electron shows | Yes (Davisson–Germer diffraction) | Yes (cathode rays, charge/mass) |
| Governing relation | λ = h/mv | E = hν, p = mv |

**Similarity:** the same entity exhibits both — **dual nature**; which face appears depends on the experiment.

**Orbit (Bohr) vs orbital (quantum)**

| Basis | Orbit | Orbital |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | Definite circular path | 3-D probability region |
| Certainty | Exact position claimed | Uncertainty principle obeyed |
| Quantum numbers | n only | n, l, mₗ (labelled by four with spin) |
| Shape | Circle | s spherical, p dumbbell, … |
| Max electrons | 2n² per shell | 2 per orbital |

## 6. Common Confusions

**ψ vs ψ²:** ψ is the wave function (no direct physical meaning); **ψ² is the probability density** — the measurable one. Quoting ψ as "probability" loses the mark.

**Diffraction vs scattering:** diffraction is wave-bending around/through regular arrays (needs wavelength ~ spacing); scattering is any direction change. Davisson–Germer is diffraction — the wave proof.
**de Broglie applies to everything:** the relation is universal; for cricket balls λ is simply too small to matter. Saying "large objects have no wavelength" is wrong — they have unobservable ones.

summary: de Broglie (1924) turned Bohr's postulate into physics: every moving particle has wavelength λ = h/mv, so an orbiting electron is a wave that survives only when a whole number of wavelengths fits its circumference (2πr = nλ) — which rearranges exactly to Bohr's mvr = nh/2π. Davisson and Germer (1927) proved it by diffracting electrons off nickel. Schrödinger's wave equation built the quantum mechanical model on this foundation: wave functions ψ whose squares give probability clouds — **orbitals** — replacing Bohr's exact orbits, which the uncertainty principle had outlawed. An electron at 10⁶ m/s has λ ≈ 0.73 nm (atomic scale, observable); a cricket ball has λ ≈ 10⁻³⁴ m (unobservable) — dual nature is universal, its visibility is not.
